claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, Rhubarb Lip Sync's own code is under the MIT licence (Copyright (c) 2015-2016 Daniel Wolf). The Summary at the top of its LICENSE.md, which the file itself calls "not legally binding", says that when you run Rhubarb on an audio file "the resulting lip sync data belongs to you alone". It adds that a video game or similar product "that doesn't ship with lip sync functionality" does not "even have to care about the MIT license". So a game that ships only the generated cue data need not carry the licence. The binding MIT text points the same way: it asks for the notice only in "copies or substantial portions of the Software", and cue data is neither. A game that ships the rhubarb binary or its code, for example to lip-sync at runtime, must carry the MIT notice and the notices of the bundled third-party parts listed in the same file: Boost, the CMU Sphinx acoustic model, PocketSphinx, sphinxbase, Flite, WebRTC, utf8proc and its Unicode data, libogg, libvorbis and others. (Checked against LICENSE.md on master, unchanged since 2025-02-17, and the v1.14.0 Linux release, 2025-04-03.)

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15 (latest release v1.14.0, 2025-04-03; LICENSE.md on master is byte-identical to the v1.14.0 copy and has not been relicensed): the code of Rhubarb Lip Sync is MIT. Every third-party component compiled into the `rhubarb` command-line binary or shipped in its `res/sphinx` data uses a permissive licence. The components are PocketSphinx and sphinxbase (variants of 2-clause BSD, CMU), the CMU Sphinx US English acoustic model (a 2-clause BSD variant, Alpha Cephei), Flite 1.4 (BSD-like, CMU), Boost and UTF8-CPP (Boost Software License), C++ Format/cppformat (2-clause BSD; the project is now called {fmt}), GSL, TCLAP and the Sound Change Applier (MIT), libogg 1.3.3, libvorbis 1.3.6 and WebRTC (3-clause BSD), utf8proc 2.2.0 (MIT, with its data under the 1991-2007 Unicode permission notice) and Where Am I? (WTFPLv2). Flite's licence has four conditions: keep the notice, clearly mark any modifications, do not delete the original authors' names, and do not use the authors' names to endorse or promote derived products without written permission. A few Flite files carry other permissive notices, for example Henry Spencer's regex ("altered versions must be plainly marked") and Markus Mummert's rateconv. That list covers only the CLI binary, not the whole release archive. Rhubarb-Lip-Sync-1.14.0-Linux.zip also contains extras/EsotericSoftwareSpine/rhubarb-for-spine-1.14.0.jar. That is a fat JAR that bundles OpenJFX 15.0.1 (GPL-2.0 with Classpath Exception, including native .so libraries), GlassFish javax.json 1.1.4 (dual CDDL-1.1/GPL-2.0), and Kotlin stdlib/reflect, TornadoFX 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT, Klaxon 5.5, Apache Commons Lang 3.12.0 and JetBrains annotations 13.0 (Apache-2.0). LICENSE.md lists none of these. Redistribute only the `rhubarb` binary, `res/` and LICENSE.md, not the extras. Lip-sync data that Rhubarb produces belongs to the user.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15 (Rhubarb Lip Sync v1.14.0, released 2025-04-03; master is still at that release commit, 9b9573cd), Rhubarb takes a WAVE (.wav) or Ogg Vorbis (.ogg) file, chosen by file extension, plus an optional --dialogFile plain-text (ASCII or UTF-8) file. It outputs a mouth-cue timeline using shapes A-F plus the optional G, H and X (the default is --extendedShapes GHX). The formats are: TSV (the default), which writes one line per cue start (timestamp in seconds, a tab, then the shape letter) and then one extra closing line holding the end-of-recording timestamp and X, or A when X is not enabled; XML; JSON (metadata.soundFile as an absolute path, metadata.duration, and a mouthCues array of {start, end, value}); or Moho/OpenToonz DAT, controlled by --datFrameRate (default 24, allowed range 24-100 fps) and --datUsePrestonBlair. The default pocketSphinx recogniser only recognises English dialog. The phonetic recogniser is described as language-independent but "usually less precise", and in v1.14.0 it ignores --dialogFile.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15 (Rhubarb Lip Sync 1.14.0, master commit 9b9573c): Rhubarb has two recognisers, chosen with -r/--recognizer. pocketSphinx is the default and recognises English only. phonetic is language-independent, but its results are "usually less precise". Rhubarb reads WAVE (.wav) and Ogg Vorbis (.ogg) input and picks the reader from the file extension. With -d/--dialogFile you pass a plain-text transcript (ASCII or UTF-8), and Rhubarb still recognises the words itself but prefers words and phrases that appear in the transcript. This only works with the pocketSphinx recogniser: the phonetic recogniser ignores the dialog file, so a transcript does nothing for non-English audio.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15: MFA needs each audio file paired with a transcript that has the same name apart from the extension. The transcript can be a .lab file (or .txt as a fallback) in Prosodylab format, or a .TextGrid for longer recordings. `mfa align CORPUS_DIRECTORY DICTIONARY_PATH ACOUSTIC_MODEL_PATH OUTPUT_DIRECTORY` writes TextGrid files with aligned words and phones by default (--output_format long_textgrid; short_textgrid, json and csv are also available). The current release is MFA 3.4.2 (2026-08-20). It installs from conda-forge (`conda create -n aligner -c conda-forge montreal-forced-aligner`) or from the mmcauliffe/montreal-forced-aligner Docker image (tag v3.4.2 or latest). Alignment itself runs on Kaldi/Kalpy and has no CUDA flag. PyTorch and a GPU are optional, and only the torch-based extras use them through --cuda: SpeechBrain (VAD segmentation, speaker diarization, transcription) and Whisper transcription (`mfa transcribe_whisper`). Since 3.4, `mfa align` in this form is deprecated. In MFA 4.0 (planned for the end of 2026) it becomes `mfa align_legacy` and `mfa align` takes the `mfa align_hf` signature (CORPUS_DIRECTORY MODEL_ID OUTPUT_DIRECTORY). `mfa align_legacy` is to be removed in MFA 5.0 (planned for 2027).
claims.as_first_reported: MFA requires paired audio and transcript files with the same basename, and `mfa align corpus dictionary acoustic_model outdir` writes TextGrid files with aligned words and phones; version 3.4 installs from conda-forge or the mmcauliffe/montreal-forced-aligner Docker image, with GPU only optional for the SpeechBrain path.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, facebook/wav2vec2-lv-60-espeak-cv-ft is marked Apache-2.0 in its Hugging Face model card metadata (`license: apache-2.0`). The repo has no LICENSE file, and the last commit is ae45363 from 2023-10-31. It is a Wav2Vec2ForCTC checkpoint (vocab_size 392), fine-tuned on multilingual Common Voice (26 languages, per fairseq) with labels made by the eSpeak phonemizer. It expects 16 kHz audio and outputs space-separated phoneme tokens. Most tokens are IPA, but 103 of the 392 carry eSpeak or tone-number marks such as 'a4', 'i5' and 'ts.h'. The vocabulary has no word-delimiter token, so the model gives no words and no word boundaries: the card says a separate dictionary is needed to map phonemes to words. Phoneme timing is available, though. The model produces CTC logits every 20 ms (320-sample stride). The Transformers tokenizer the checkpoint uses, Wav2Vec2PhonemeCTCTokenizer, returns start and end frame offsets for each phoneme through decode/batch_decode(..., output_char_offsets=True), and the ASR pipeline does the same with return_timestamps="char". This timing is approximate, because CTC predictions come as short spikes. Phonemes can therefore be timed without a separate aligner, but word timing still needs one.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, the NVIDIA/Audio2Face-3D-SDK README lists these requirements: Windows 10/11 or Linux (Ubuntu 20.04+), an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA 12.8.0+ support, CUDA >=12.8 and <13.0 (12.9 recommended), TensorRT >=10.13 and <11.0, Python 3.8 to 3.10.x, 8GB+ RAM and 4GB+ GPU memory recommended. The Audio2Face-3D-v3.0 model card (on Hugging Face since 09/24/2025, NVIDIA Open Model License) describes the output as "Facial motion", format "Array of float", "Two-Dimensional (2D)", with "Facial motion on skin, tongue, jaw, and eyeballs". The card never mentions blendshapes or ARKit. The v3.0 model repo does ship blendshape-solve data, though. For each of three identities (Claire, James, Mark) it has a bs_skin npz with 52 ARKit-named poses (eyeBlinkLeft through tongueOut) on a 24,002-vertex skin mesh, and a bs_tongue npz with 16 tongue poses. model.json lists these under "blendshapePaths". The SDK docs say the geometry output "can optionally be converted to blendshape weights using a specialized solver", through its CPU and GPU blendshape executors. So the model plus the SDK can produce ARKit-named blendshape weights locally, with no NIM microservice. The solver fits against NVIDIA's own identity meshes, so the weights only drive a character that already has matching ARKit blendshapes.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, uLipSync (github.com/hecomi/uLipSync, default branch main, package com.hecomi.ulipsync v3.1.5) is under the MIT License, "Copyright (c) 2021 hecomi". That covers the plug-in code. Two things are not MIT: the optional samples include Unity-chan assets ("© Unity Technologies Japan/UCL", under the Unity-Chan License), and the plug-in needs Unity's com.unity.burst and com.unity.mathematics packages, which use the Unity Companion License. uLipSync is a C# plug-in that runs only in Unity (UnityEngine, Job System, Burst). The uLipSync component takes the AudioSource buffer in OnAudioFilterRead() (AudioClip.GetData() on WebGL), computes 12 MFCCs and scores them against the MFCCs saved for each phoneme in a Profile ScriptableObject, using L1, L2 or cosine distance. You name the phonemes and there are no defaults: a new Profile is empty. The README suggests A, I, U, E, O plus a breath phoneme such as "-". The repo ships sample Male, Female and Unity-chan profiles that you can recalibrate from a mic or an AudioClip. The seven-item "A, I, U, E, O, N, -" list in the README is only the Unity-chan sample's phoneme-to-blendshape table. The result can drive four kinds of target: blendshapes on a SkinnedMeshRenderer (uLipSyncBlendShape), textures or UVs (uLipSyncTexture), AnimatorController parameters (uLipSyncAnimator), or VRM avatars. VRM uses uLipSyncBlendShapeVRM for VRM 0.x VRMBlendShapeProxy and uLipSyncExpressionVRM for VRM 1.0 expressions; both are in the "04. VRM" sample, not the core runtime. In the Editor, audio can be pre-baked into BakedData ScriptableObjects, played on a Timeline uLipSync Track, or turned into AnimationClips. It does not run outside Unity.
claims.as_first_reported: uLipSync is MIT (Copyright (c) 2021 hecomi) and is a Unity plug-in that compares MFCCs of the playing audio against user-calibrated phoneme profiles (default A, I, U, E, O, N and '-' for noise) to produce blendshape weights on SkinnedMeshRenderer or VRM 0.x/1.0 expressions, with optional pre-baking to BakedData ScriptableObjects, Timeline or AnimationClips; it does not run outside Unity.

As of 2026-09-15, Rhubarb Lip Sync 1.14.0 (released 2025-04-03 and still the latest release) uses six basic mouth shapes, A to F, which you must always draw. Its README says these six were invented at the Hanna-Barbera studios. There are also three optional extended shapes: G, H and X. The shapes are: A closed mouth for P, B and M, with slight pressure between the lips. B slightly open with clenched teeth, for most consonants (K, S, T) and some vowels such as EE. C open, for EH and AE and some consonants, and also the in-between from A or B to D. D wide open, for AA. E slightly rounded, for AO and ER, and also the in-between from C or D to F. F puckered, for UW, OW and W. G upper teeth touching the lower lip, for F and V. H for long L sounds, with the tongue raised behind the upper teeth. X idle or rest, with the lips closed but relaxed, used for pauses. The --extendedShapes option defaults to "GHX", and an empty string "" limits output to A-F. The shapes use Rhubarb's own letter names. Preston Blair names (MBP, etc, E, AI, O, U, FV, L, rest) are only an optional renaming when exporting .dat files with --datUsePrestonBlair.

claims.claim: (Checked 2026-09-15.) Source keeps a voice line's lip-sync data inside the .wav file itself, as an ASCII text block in a custom RIFF chunk called "VDAT" (riff.h: WAVE_VALVEDATA = MAKEID('V','D','A','T')). The block reads: VERSION 1.0; PLAINTEXT { transcript }; WORDS { WORD <word> <start> <end> { <phoneme code> <phoneme name> <start> <end> <volume> ... } ... }; EMPHASIS { <time> <value> ... }; OPTIONS { voice_duck <0|1> [checksum <n>] }. Times are in seconds, written to 3 decimal places. The phoneme code is a character code: plain ASCII for simple sounds (100 = d) and the IPA Unicode code point otherwise (593 = U+0251 for aa, 952 = U+03B8 for th). The fifth phoneme field is a "volume" that nothing uses: the parser reads it and throws it away, and Valve's writer always prints 1. The weight used for each phoneme comes from the engine's own phoneme table (WeightForPhonemeCode in phonemeconverter.cpp), not from the file. Older files may also carry a CLOSECAPTION section, which the SDK parser now skips ("CLOSECAPTION IS NO LONGER VALID").

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, Live2D Cubism has two lip-sync routes, and only the basic one is driven by volume. (1) Basic lip-sync (volume): the application gets an audio level "in some way" and passes a value from 0 to 1 through CubismModel SetParameterValue/AddParameterValue to the parameters listed in the .model3.json Groups entry named "LipSync" (the Editor exports ["ParamMouthOpenY"] by default). The SDK framework reads those IDs through GetLipSyncParameterCount/GetLipSyncParameterId, but it does not measure the audio itself. Values outside 0 to 1 raise no error, though lip-sync "may not operate properly". In the Editor, Animation > Apply Lip-sync from the Audio File (WAV only) adds volume keyframes to the model track's Lip-sync property group, which also has Scale, Default Value (a threshold) and Effect settings (SDK Lip-sync page updated 01/29/2026; Editor page updated 05/21/2024). (2) Motion-sync (visemes): Cubism Editor 5 and the separate Cubism SDK MotionSync Plugin turn audio into a time series of visemes (Silence, A, I, U, E, O) using CRI LipSync, then blend shapes the user has mapped for each viseme. The settings are stored in .motionsync3.json and can be baked to keyframes in the Editor (pages updated 10/17/2023 and 12/19/2023). The Standard Parameter List (updated 08/26/2021) has only two mouth parameters, ParamMouthForm (-1 to 1, default 0) and ParamMouthOpenY (0 to 1, default 0), and no vowel or viseme parameters. Even so, motion-sync's "Basic" preset drives vowels through those two parameters, and its "Vowels only (blend shape)" preset expects a custom parameter for each viseme. The MotionSync Plugin is proprietary: its Core is not on GitHub and it is covered by the Live2D Proprietary Software License Agreement. Live2D lists no official Linux support for it on Native or Unity.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, Blender's Data Transfer modifier (Blender 4.5 LTS, the bpy version in the container, and still true on Blender main) can copy the following from a source mesh. Vertex data: vertex groups, bevel weights and colour attributes. Edge data: sharp marks, UV seams, subdivision creases, bevel weights and Freestyle edge marks. It cannot copy shape keys: in 4.5 the "Shapekey(s)" option is disabled in the source with `#if 0 /* TODO */`, and on main it has been removed. So it is the right tool for copying jaw (vertex-group) weights onto a mesh, and the wrong one for blendshapes.

The test mesh was an ico sphere with 642 vertices, not a generated character. The jaw bone was a child of a bone named "head". Vertices below z=-0.3 and toward the front (y<0.1) got jaw weight, fading in over 0.3 units. Rotating the jaw 20 degrees moved 123 of 642 vertices by more than 0.01. A "jawOpen" shape key was copied onto the mesh from a UV-sphere template with the Surface Deform modifier (bind, then "apply as shape key"; the new key comes out named "sd" and was renamed "jawOpen"). The mesh and armature were exported with export_scene.gltf(export_morph=True) and Blender's default Apply Modifiers=off, then imported again. Everything survived: bones [head, jaw] with jaw still parented to head, vertex groups [head, jaw], shape keys [Basis, jawOpen] with the same maximum displacement (0.304), and a working Armature modifier. The mesh came back with 3840 vertices instead of 642, because vertices are split per face, so vertex indices do not survive the round trip.

claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15 (Blender main, and the same on the blender-v4.5-release branch that bpy 4.5 uses): the Human metarig that Rigify adds (metarigs/human.py) puts the legacy, deprecated `faces.super_face` rig type on its 'face' bone, not the modular face. It needs every named face child to exist under 'face': nose, lip.T/B.L/R, jaw, ear.L/R, brow.B.L/R, lid.T.L/R, forehead.L/R (plus .001/.002), eye.L/R, cheek.T.L/R, teeth.T/B, tongue and temple.L/R. The modular jaw rig `face.skin_jaw` only appears after you run Pose > "Upgrade Face Rig" (pose.rigify_upgrade_face). That operator adds a 'jaw_master' bone of type face.skin_jaw and turns the lip.T/B.L/R bones into skin.stretchy_chain rigs. The docstring of face.skin_jaw reads "Jaw rig that manages loops of four mouth chains each. The chains must connect together at their ends using L/R and T/B symmetry". The manual adds that it needs "one or more child chain loops, each formed by four skin chains tagged with .T/.B and .L/.R". If no mouth corners are found, generation stops with "Could not find all mouth corners". Whichever face rig you use, the metarig's face bones (jaw, jaw.L/R, chin, teeth.T/B, tongue, lip, lid, brow, cheek, nose, ear, forehead, temple, eye) start at fixed human-sized coordinates. Rigify cannot fit them automatically, so you have to move them by hand to match the character's mesh. Where two or more bone ends meet at the same point, they must still meet after the move.

It only allows non-commercial scientific research, non-commercial education or non-commercial artistic projects. It forbids commercial use ("incorporation in a commercial product"), redistribution, and training models for commercial use. A commercial licence has to be negotiated through ps-license@tue.mpg.de. Only the FLAME 2023 Open model (released November 2025) is under the "Open Model License". The site calls it CC-BY-4.0, and it allows sharing and adapting "for any purpose, including commercial use". It still requires attribution (credit, a link to the licence, and a note of any changes). It also adds two limits that plain CC BY 4.0 does not have: no pornographic use, and no fake, libellous, misleading or defamatory content. claims.claim: As of 2026-09-15, ICT-FaceKit's public release (github.com/USC-ICT/ICT-FaceKit, master branch, last commit da5f95a on 2020-12-01, no tagged releases) is MIT licensed, "Copyright (c) 2020 USC Institute for Creative Technologies". The MIT notice is also embedded in the OBJ data files, so the licence covers the mesh and morph-target data as well as the code, and shipping them requires including that notice. The release contains the "ICT Face Model Light": a 26,719-vertex, 26,384-face head topology (face, head and neck, mouth and eye sockets, gums and tongue, teeth, eyeballs, lacrimal fluid, eye blend and occlusion meshes, eyelashes). It also has 100 identity PCA morph targets (identity000-099.obj) and 53 expression shapes that use ARKit-style names with _L/_R suffixes (browInnerUp and cheekPuff split left and right, no tongueOut), listed in vertex_indices.json. The folder holds 4 more shapes the loader does not read (PupilDilate_L/R, cheekRaiser_L/R). There is a Blender add-on script (Blender/Scripts/ICTFaceKit.py) that imports these and joins them as shape keys, but it calls bpy.ops.import_scene.obj, which does not exist in Blender 4.5, so it must be changed to bpy.ops.wm.obj_import before it runs in this pipeline. The README says the "Full ICT Face Model" (200+ identity and albedo modes, FBX face rig) "will be released under a different USC specific license"; it is not in the repository.

(Checked 2026-09-15.) In his Filmic Worlds post "Solving Blendshapes for ARKit" (John Hable, 14 November 2021), Hable released colin_shape_data.zip under CC0 1.0 Universal. - The separate Daz to Roblox Supplemental Terms (a Roblox Reseller License per asset, or a $9.99/month subscription for Daz Originals) allow Genesis content inside Roblox, and nowhere else.

A signed agreement with Daz replaces the EULA, and a product page can add further rights or restrictions.

As of 2026-09-15: Celeste's Portraits.xml is a Monocle SpriteBank. Each <portrait_NAME path sfx textbox> element holds an <sfxs> list that gives each expression an audio index, plus animation entries that are either <Loop> (repeats) or <Anim> (plays once, with an optional goto). Both take id, path, delay and frames. frames is a frame list with ranges and repeats, such as "0-9" or "0*6"; leave it out to use every frame. Animation ids take one of three prefixes plus the expression name. begin_ is played before the idle or talk animation, and the textbox waits for it to finish, so in practice it must be an <Anim>. idle_ is played when not talking, and talk_ is played when talking. In dialogue files, markup such as [THEO left normal] (vanilla English.txt, CH2_THEO_B) picks the character (portrait_theo), the side (left or right) and the expression (normal). The parser also accepts the optional flags flip, upsidedown and pop. Sources: EverestAPI/Resources wiki, Custom-Portraits page (last edited 2025-08-29) and Adding-Custom-Dialogue page.

As of 2026-09-15, diffusers ships QwenImageEditInpaintPipeline. It was added in PR #12225 (merged 2025-08-31), first released in v0.36.0 (2025-12-08), is unchanged in v0.40.0 (2026-08-20, the current PyPI release), and is exported as `from diffusers import QwenImageEditInpaintPipeline`. Its __call__ takes image, mask_image and strength (0 to 1; the signature default is 0.6 even though the docstring says 1.0). In mask_image, white pixels are repainted and black pixels are kept. The mask is turned into pure black and white at 0.5 and shrunk to the latent grid (1/8 resolution). At every denoising step the latents outside the mask are reset to the original image's latents, so a mouth-only edit stays inside the mask and the rest of the portrait is not re-diffused. Three limits apply. First, the whole image is always resized to about 1 megapixel (calculate_dimensions(1024*1024, aspect ratio)), and the height and width arguments are overwritten. Second, the whole image goes through the VAE, so without padding_mask_crop the unmasked pixels come back as a VAE reconstruction, not an exact copy. Third, the original pixels are only pasted back outside the mask when padding_mask_crop is set, which needs PIL inputs, output_type="pil", and a mask the same size as the resized image. The pipeline is built for Qwen/Qwen-Image-Edit and has a single-image prompt template. diffusers has no Edit-Plus (2509/2511) inpaint variant.

claims.claim: [LIP-130] As of 2026-09-15, canopylabs/orpheus-3b-0.1-ft on Hugging Face still carries the tag license:apache-2.0 (card last changed 2025-05-06). Its card metadata lists meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as a base model, next to canopylabs/orpheus-3b-0.1-pretrained. Canopy Labs' own pretraining config starts from meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. In GitHub issues #29 and #33 (March to April 2025), a Canopy Labs collaborator said the Apache-2.0 tag was wrong. They said the weights come under the Llama licence as a derivative work, and that only the GitHub code is Apache-2.0. The Hugging Face tag was never corrected. Treat the weights as bound by the Llama 3.2 Community License (version dated 2024-09-25), not Apache-2.0. That licence requires anyone who distributes the weights or a product containing them to include a copy of the agreement and to prominently display "Built with Llama". It also requires "Llama" at the start of the name of any derived model that is distributed. The Orpheus release does none of this: its Hugging Face repo has no licence file, its card never says "Built with Llama", and the name has no "Llama" prefix. A game that ships these weights has to meet those terms itself. Apache-2.0 covers only the Orpheus-TTS code.

It arrived in commit daa9b4f3, 'S2 beta (#1164)', on 2026-03-10, and is also the licence on tag v2.0.0-beta. The README says the codebase and its model weights are both released under it. Its code is MIT, but the LICENSE file adds a third-party model licence table, so GitHub's licence detector reports NOASSERTION. Its README lists "19 Engines". 16 are TTS engines, including Qwen3-TTS, ChatterBox/ChatterBox 23L, F5-TTS, IndexTTS 2/2.5, Fish Audio S2 Pro and MOSS-TTS. The other three are Granite ASR (speech recognition), MOSS-SoundEffect v2 (sound effects) and RVC (voice conversion). The README calls only Echo-TTS non-commercial in so many words ("CC-BY-NC-SA"). For Fish Audio S2 Pro and DramaBox it just gives the licence names (Fish Audio Research License, LTX-2 Community License). The full commercial-use flags are in the LICENSE file's "Third-Party Model Licenses" table, not the README. That table marks F5-TTS (CC-BY-NC-4.0), VibeVoice (research-only per model card), Higgs Audio v3, Echo-TTS and Fish Audio S2 Pro as "No". It marks Higgs Audio 2, IndexTTS 2/2.5, Step Audio EditX and DramaBox as "Conditional", and RVC community models as "Varies". The README's installation prerequisites say "Python 3.12 or higher". That is above the repo's Python 3.11 container, so the pack is not supported there. However, install.py does not check the Python version and pyproject.toml sets no requires-python, so nothing blocks an install on 3.11. It is unsupported and untested there, not proven to fail.

claims.claim: (Checked 2026-09-15, Rhubarb Lip Sync 1.14.0, Linux build.) Rhubarb's `dat` exporter writes Moho/OpenToonz switch data files, which start with the header `MohoSwitch1`. It only accepts `--datFrameRate` values from 24 to 100 fps, both included, and the default is 24. `--datFrameRate 12` exits with code 1 and the message 'Frame rate must be between 24 and 100 fps.', so it cannot produce a 12 fps sprite timeline directly. With `--threads 1`, the 88-row file came out every time. `--datUsePrestonBlair` only renames the shapes after the animation is made, and the frame numbers stay the same. The mapping is A→MBP, B→etc, C→E, D→AI, E→O, F→U, G→FV, H→L, X→rest. Note that the Preston Blair name 'E' is Rhubarb's shape C, while Rhubarb's shape E becomes 'O'.
